source.title: Towards a theory of how the structure of language is acquired by deep neural networks

record.tranche_reason: Measures held-out cross-entropy as training-set size changes, testing loss-versus-data scaling in a different setup from the original scaling-law studies. It does not sweep parameter count or compute.
record.gate_note: The paper cites earlier scaling-law work, but cited results are not recorded as rows. The paper’s own analytical account of correlations and hidden representations is described in the text, but rows below focus on its reported learning-curve results. Real-text experiments vary character-context length and training-set size; the plots do not give exact loss values.
record.test_reason: The study trains small transformers and CNNs on synthetic PCFG data and on character-level tinyShakespeare and WikiText-103. It measures held-out cross-entropy against training-set size P. On real text it reports a power law L∼P^-α (α≃0.1 and α≃0.095) that levels off at a context-length-dependent P*(t)∼t^z. That bears directly on V1 for the data axis, and on V7's claim that curves bend away from a single power law. It does not sweep parameters or compute. Its restatement L(P,t)=t^-αz f(P/t^z) has some T5 character.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right, with two additions. The authors argue that more data lets models resolve longer-range correlations and build deeper hierarchical representations, producing loss steps on synthetic data that together make up a power law. In their theory, the exponent depends on the data structure. On Shakespeare and Wikipedia, the conjectured link between training-set size and effective context predicts where the loss power law saturates, and the loss collapse confirms Eq. 16.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies training-set size in synthetic hierarchical data and character-level text using last-token prediction; it does not reproduce the original studies’ parameter-count or compute sweeps. The empirical curves also include finite-context plateaus and, for RHM, stepwise changes.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss-curve saturation depends on context-window length. The empirical decay exponent is reported as corpus- and tokenisation-dependent. CNN and transformer learning curves are qualitatively similar but differ quantitatively; the CNN third step occurs with less training data than predicted in one reported comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: In depth-3 CNNs on RHM, the first and second loss steps collapse when P is rescaled by the predicted thresholds P1 and P2=vm^3 as m varies (Figs 7–8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample complexity of each loss step in hierarchical data scales as v·m^(2ℓ−1).

fits_no_version.finding: Hidden representations become invariant to subtree resampling at the same Pℓ as the loss steps (Fig. 3). The first step's sample complexity also scales linearly with context size, P1∝(t+1) (Fig. 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss steps coincide with emergence of representations of deeper hidden variables.

record.problems: The study uses simplified synthetic grammar assumptions and only two character-level text datasets for its real-text test. It states that there is no proof connecting its proposed strategy to gradient-descent training of deep networks, and notes quantitative architecture discrepancies. Loss values are presented in plots without exact values in the text; no error bars or confidence intervals are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No reported loss-scaling conditions were omitted. Correlation estimates, hidden-representation probes, and analytical mechanisms are not rows for the listed versions because they do not themselves measure the held-out-loss scaling named by those versions.

untested.parts: Scaling in parameters and compute; large-scale LM training; power law over more than ~2–3 decades of data.
All of it; the authors list compute-optimal allocation as future work.
Effects of parameter counting, schedule and fitting method on exponents; the compute-optimal split. Corpus dependence of the loss exponent is not shown empirically (α≃0.1 vs 0.095).

missing.what: Fitted loss exponents: α≃0.1 (tinyShakespeare) and α≃0.095 (WikiText-103). Rows give only 'figure only'.
missing.locator: Fig. 4 top left; Fig. 5 top left

missing.what: The loss collapse under L·t^αz vs P/t^z, with z≃2.8 (Shakespeare) and z≃3.1 (Wiki) taken from the correlation decay. This quantifies where the bend occurs.
missing.locator: Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 bottom left; Eq. 16

missing.what: Statement that increasing layers or heads (and RHM heads 16→64) does not change results. This indicates parameters were not the bottleneck in the data sweeps.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V7 reason wrongly attributes the 'exponent depends on corpus and tokenisation' footnote to the loss exponent; it refers to the correlation exponent β (1.4 vs 1.55). The loss exponents are nearly equal (0.1 vs 0.095). Training uses multi-epoch training to convergence with best-validation model selection. P is a number of (t+1)-character examples, not tokens in single-pass training. Models are small (at most ~10M parameters). The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Parameter-count and compute scaling; token-count scaling in conventional large-scale language-model training; whether the power law holds when other scaling variables are not bottlenecks.

Parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, and compute-optimal allocation choices; the study does not compare published fits or estimate alternative exponents under different fitting methods.
